$comment: California commercial statutes. These are the provisions that override ordinary contract drafting when a California party or a California consumer is involved — automatic renewal, choice of law for employees, releases, and service provider data terms.

clauses.title: California Automatic Renewal Requirements
clauses.rationale: California's automatic renewal law is prescriptive about presentation, consent, and cancellation. Non-compliant renewals can be treated as unconditional gifts, and the statute carries a private right of action.
clauses.body: California's [[automatic renewal law]] reaches offers made to a CONSUMER — an individual acquiring goods, services, money or credit for personal, family or household purposes — so it does not govern a business-to-business subscription, and the renewal in <<xr:msa_renewal>> is outside it unless the counterparty buys as a consumer. Where it does apply, the automatic renewal or continuous service offer terms must be presented clearly and conspicuously before the agreement is fulfilled and in visual proximity — temporal proximity, for a voice offer — to the request for consent; the business must obtain the consumer's express affirmative consent to those terms and must not include anything in the contract that undermines the ability to give it; and an acknowledgment containing the terms, the cancellation policy and how to cancel must be provided in a form the consumer can retain. Verification of consent must be kept for at least three (3) years, or one (1) year after termination, whichever is longer. A pre-renewal notice is required in two cases only: where the consumer took a free gift or trial, or a promotional price, lasting more than thirty-one (31) days, in which case it goes out between twenty-one (21) and three (3) days before that period expires; and where the initial term is one year or longer, in which case it goes out between forty-five (45) and fifteen (15) days before renewal. A consumer who signed up online must be able to cancel exclusively online through a prominent direct link or button, or an immediately accessible pre-formatted termination email, without further obstruction, and cancellation must be available in the same medium the consumer used. A retention offer may be presented on the way out only if a "click to cancel" link is displayed alongside it, or, by telephone, only after the consumer is told they can complete cancellation at any time by saying so. Notify a material change with information on how to cancel, and a fee change between thirty (30) and seven (7) days before it takes effect. Send an annual reminder to a consumer on an annual plan, stating the product, the frequency and amount of the charges, and how to cancel. Two limits on exposure that a drafter should know: goods sent without first obtaining affirmative consent are deemed an unconditional gift, but that consequence attaches to goods and to the absence of consent, not to every non-compliance; and a business that complies with the article in good faith is not subject to civil remedies. There is no private right of action under this article — a Court of Appeal has so held — so a consumer's route is the unfair competition law or an action by the Attorney General. The amendments described here apply only to a contract entered into, amended or extended on or after 1 July 2025, and the article exempts entities regulated by the Public Utilities Commission, the FCC or FERC, the Department of Insurance, alarm company operators, banks and other licensed financial institutions, and regulated service contract sellers.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§17600–17606, read as a whole (§§17601 and 17602 as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 515 (AB 2863))
CourtListener — Mayron v. Google LLC (Cal. Ct. App. 2020)

defects: The clause is inserted whenever the agreement auto-renews and the counterparty is Californian. Because the article reaches only consumers, that condition fires the clause for business-to-business agreements it does not govern. The rebuilt body says so in its first sentence rather than changing the condition, which is an engine change nobody has approved.

The clause states that a business complying in good faith is not subject to civil remedies (§17604(b)). No decision construing that safe harbour was read, and it is the kind of provision whose scope is decided by case law rather than text.
The interaction between this article and the federal Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, and any FTC negative-option rule, was not researched. A national subscription business needs both.

clauses.title: California Choice of Law Limits
clauses.rationale: A commercial choice-of-law clause is generally enforceable between businesses, but it does not carry over to individuals working in California — which is where companies with contractor networks get caught.
clauses.body: Between businesses a governing law clause is generally enforceable, and California expressly permits the parties to a contract relating to a transaction involving in the aggregate not less than two hundred fifty thousand dollars ($250,000) to agree that California law governs, whether or not the transaction bears a reasonable relation to this state. Read that permission narrowly: it validates the choice of California law, not the choice of another state's; and it does not apply to a contract for labor or personal services, to a transaction primarily for personal, family or household purposes, or to the extent Commercial Code section 1301(c) provides otherwise. The freedom does not extend to individuals. Labor Code section 925 makes a provision voidable where an employer requires an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to adjudicate a California claim outside California or to give up the substantive protection of California law in a California controversy; adjudication includes arbitration. The provision is voidable at the employee's election, not void, and if voided at their request the matter is adjudicated in California under California law. Section 925 applies only to a contract entered into, modified or extended on or after January 1, 2017, and does not apply where the employee was in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the venue, forum or choice-of-law term — which is the one lawful route to a non-California forum. Where individuals perform under this Agreement in California, do not assume the selected forum reaches them, and note that section 925 speaks of employees: whether it reaches a contractor who is later found to have been misclassified was not verified and is not asserted here.

Whether §925 is preempted by the Federal Arbitration Act where the covered provision is an arbitration clause was not researched and is not addressed. For a commercial agreement that arbitrates, that is the question that decides whether the clause matters.

Civil Code §1646.5 permits choosing California law. Nothing read here validates a choice of another state's law in a California-connected commercial contract, which is the more common drafting problem. The clause states the limit and does not answer the question.

clauses.title: California Anti-Indemnity Limits
clauses.rationale: California voids broad-form indemnity in construction contracts. A clause copied from a general commercial template is unenforceable in this context and can invalidate the additional insured position with it.
clauses.body: Two provisions do different work here. Civil Code section 2782(a) makes void and unenforceable a provision in a construction contract that purports to indemnify the promisee against liability arising from the promisee's own SOLE negligence or wilful misconduct, or from defects in design furnished by the promisee or those directly responsible to it — subject to the exceptions in sections 2782.1, 2782.2, 2782.5 and 2782.6, and without affecting the validity of an insurance contract issued by an admitted insurer. Section 2782.05 goes further for contracts entered into on or after 1 January 2013: a subcontractor's indemnity of a general contractor, construction manager or other subcontractor is void and unenforceable TO THE EXTENT the claims arise out of, pertain to, or relate to that party's ACTIVE negligence or wilful misconduct, to defects in design it furnished, or to work outside the subcontractor's contractual scope. "To the extent" is the operative phrase and a Court of Appeal has held it means what it says: a general contractor whose active negligence contributed to the loss is not barred from all indemnity, only from indemnity for the portion of liability attributable to that active negligence. The indemnity in <<xr:msa_indemnity_mutual>> is limited accordingly. Section 2782.05 cannot be waived or modified, and California law applies to every contract within it notwithstanding any choice-of-law provision to the contrary — so naming another state's law does not escape it. Do not assume the same limits reach the insurance programme: section 2782.05 expressly does not apply to a wrap-up policy or programme, or to a provision requiring the promisor to purchase or maintain insurance covering the promisor's own acts and omissions, including additional insured endorsements for ongoing and completed operations. Section 2782.05 also does not apply to residential construction subject to Title 7, to direct contracts with a public agency or a private owner (which section 2782(b) and (c) govern instead, on an active-negligence standard), or to contracts with design professionals. Finally, a defence obligation is triggered by a written tender: on receiving one the subcontractor must elect, within thirty (30) days, either to defend with counsel of its choice or to pay a reasonable allocated share of defence costs within thirty (30) days of each invoice.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Civ. Code §2782 (Title 12, Indemnity, read as a whole)
California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Civ. Code §2782.05
CourtListener — Oltmans Construction Co. v. Bayside Interiors, Inc. (2017) 10 Cal.App.5th 355

defects: Sections 2782.1, 2782.2, 2782.5 and 2782.6 are named as exceptions to §2782(a) but their contents were not read in full; they were seen only in the Title 12 listing. A party relying on one of them gets no help from this clause.

The residential-construction regime in §2782(d)-(i) was read and is not carried, beyond the statement that §2782.05 does not reach it. A residential builder or its subcontractor needs §2782(d), which has its own standard (negligence, not active negligence), its own 90-day election period, and its own damages provisions.
Whether the §2782.05(c) choice-of-law override survives a forum outside California was not researched. The section says California law applies; it does not say a foreign court must apply it.

clauses.title: Section 1542 Waiver in Settlements
clauses.benchmark: Present in 93% of California settlement and release agreements
clauses.rationale: A general release governed by California law does not reach unknown claims unless Section 1542 is expressly waived, quoting the statute.
clauses.body: A general release does not extend to claims that the releasing party does not know or suspect to exist in their favour at the time of executing the release and that, if known, would have materially affected their settlement with the released party. That protection is a statutory benefit the releasing party may waive, and a release intended to reach unknown claims should waive it expressly and quote the section as it currently reads — the wording was amended effective 1 January 2019 to speak of the creditor or releasing party and the debtor or released party, so a form quoting the pre-2019 text quotes a section that no longer says that. Quoting is not what makes the waiver work. The purpose of section 1542 is to stop a mere recital that a release covers unknown claims from barring a claim discovered later in the absence of a showing of conscious understanding, so what the court looks for is whether this releasing party actually understood what was being given up: an express waiver, negotiated at arm's length with the advice of counsel, has been enforced against a party who later said he had not known of the claim. Draft accordingly — say what risk is being assumed, record that the party had the opportunity to take advice, and carve out by name any claim the parties mean to preserve.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Civ. Code §1542 (as amended by Stats. 2018, Ch. 157 (SB 1431), eff. Jan. 1, 2019)
California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Civ. Code §1541
California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Civ. Code §3513, the maxim under which a §1542 benefit is waivable

defects: Civil Code §3513 was read for the proposition that the benefit of §1542 is waivable, since §1542 itself says nothing about waiver. No decision was read that expressly ties §1542's waivability to §3513, so that link is this rebuild's reasoning from the two texts rather than something a court has been seen to hold.

Winet is a 1992 Court of Appeal decision and quotes §1542 in its pre-2019 wording. It is relied on only for the conscious-understanding standard it takes from Casey v. Proctor, which turns on the purpose of the section rather than on the amended words. Casey itself was not opened.
Whether a §1542 waiver reaches claims that had not yet accrued at the date of the release, as opposed to accrued claims the party did not know about, was not researched and is not addressed.

clauses.title: Proposition 65 Warnings
clauses.rationale: Enforced largely through private actions with fee recovery, which makes it a volume business for plaintiffs' counsel. Allocating responsibility up the supply chain is the practical defense.
clauses.body: Proposition 65 forbids a person in the course of doing business from knowingly and intentionally exposing any individual to a chemical known to the state to cause cancer or reproductive toxicity without first giving a clear and reasonable warning. Two thresholds decide whether it reaches a party at all. "Person in the course of doing business" does not include a person employing fewer than ten (10) employees, so a party under that headcount owes no warning — but the exemption is personal to that party and relieves no one else in the chain. And knowledge is not confined to what a seller actually knew: a Court of Appeal has held that constructive knowledge suffices, on the ground that an actual-knowledge rule would reward not looking. Allocate expressly between the parties: who determines whether a warning is required, who supplies its content and placement including on the product page, who bears the cost of the warning method, and who indemnifies a claim and defends the sixty-day notice. Set that allocation against the regulatory default, under which primary responsibility for a consumer product exposure rests on the manufacturer, producer, packager, importer or distributor rather than the retail seller, who is responsible only in limited circumstances including actual knowledge — NOT VERIFIED: that default is 27 C.C.R. §25600.2 and it was read only as quoted by the Court of Appeal in Lee v. Amazon.com, because the publisher of the California Code of Regulations, govt.westlaw.com, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy and the promulgating agency's own sites, oehha.ca.gov and p65warnings.ca.gov, return a firewall challenge instead of the text. The same caveat applies to warning content: the statute requires a warning that is "clear and reasonable", and the Article 6 regulations define the wording and methods deemed to satisfy that — a warning that departs from them is outside the safe harbour and has to be defended as clear and reasonable on the facts, which is not the same as being void. NOT VERIFIED: no Article 6 section was read from a publisher, so this Agreement should name the applicable section and a reviewer should confirm it. Three statutory exemptions apply: federal preemption of the warning, an exposure less than twelve months after the chemical was listed, and an exposure the defendant shows poses no significant risk on the statutory measure, on which the defendant carries the burden. Enforcement is by the Attorney General, a district attorney or a qualifying city attorney, or by a private person in the public interest sixty (60) days after notice served with a certificate of merit and only where no public prosecutor is diligently prosecuting; the civil penalty is up to two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per day for each violation, assessed against seven statutory factors that include whether the violator took good faith measures to comply and when it took them.

CourtListener — Lee v. Amazon.com, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 2022)

defects: The Article 6 safe-harbour regulations (27 C.C.R. §25600 and following, including §25600.2 on allocation and the internet-purchase provisions) could not be read from any publisher. govt.westlaw.com, the publisher of the California Code of Regulations, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy; oehha.ca.gov and p65warnings.ca.gov, the promulgating agency's own sites, return an Incapsula firewall challenge rather than the document. Everything this clause says about the regulations is carried behind an explicit NOT VERIFIED marker and rests on the Court of Appeal's quotation of §25600.2 in Lee v. Amazon.com — a court quoting a regulation is strong corroboration and is not the text.

The clause is conditioned on industry being ecommerce. Proposition 65 is not an ecommerce statute; a manufacturer or a physical retailer with ten or more employees is equally covered. The condition was not changed by this rebuild and it means the clause will not fire for parties who need it.

The internet-purchase warning rules — where a warning must appear relative to the purchase button, and whether a warning delivered with the product suffices — are in Article 6 and were not read. The clause tells the drafter to allocate responsibility for placement "including on the product page" without being able to say what compliant placement is.

clauses.title: CCPA Service Provider Terms
clauses.rationale: Service provider status is not a label — it depends on specific contract terms being present. Without them the transfer is a sale, which triggers opt-out rights the business almost certainly has not built.
clauses.body: To qualify as a service provider rather than a recipient of a sale of personal information, this Addendum must state the specific business purposes for processing, prohibit selling or sharing the personal information, prohibit retaining, using, or disclosing it outside the direct business relationship or for any purpose other than the specified services, prohibit combining it with information from other sources except as permitted, require notice if the service provider can no longer meet its obligations, and grant the business the right to take reasonable steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use. The roles stated in <<xr:dpa_roles>> depend on these terms being present.

clauses.title: Sensitive Personal Information
clauses.rationale: California created a distinct category with its own right to limit use, and it captures data most businesses do not think of as sensitive — precise geolocation and contents of messages among them.
clauses.body: Sensitive personal information under California law includes government identifiers, financial account credentials, precise geolocation, racial or ethnic origin, religious beliefs, union membership, the contents of mail and messages, genetic and biometric data, and health, sex life, or sexual orientation data. Consumers may direct that its use be limited to what is necessary to provide the service. Identify in the processing description at <<xr:dpa_scope>> whether any sensitive category is in scope, and implement the limitation right where it is.

clauses.title: Deletion Down the Chain
clauses.rationale: The deletion obligation flows to every subprocessor, and a business cannot satisfy a consumer request it has no mechanism to push downstream.
clauses.body: On a consumer deletion request, the {{selfLabel}} shall delete the personal information and direct each subprocessor engaged under <<xr:dpa_subprocessors>> to do the same, unless a statutory exception applies. Maintain a record of the request, the action taken, and any exception relied on. Deletion obligations reach backups on the ordinary cycle as provided in <<xr:dpa_deletion>>.

clauses.title: California Prevailing Wage
clauses.rationale: Public works reaches further than most contractors expect, including privately built projects that receive public subsidy, and the penalties are per worker per day.
clauses.body: If any part of this work is a public work under California law — including private projects paid for in whole or part with public funds — prevailing wage rates apply, contractors and subcontractors must be registered with the Department of Industrial Relations, certified payroll records must be submitted electronically, and apprenticeship requirements attach. Confirm public works status before pricing. Penalties are assessed per worker per day of violation, and the awarding body may withhold payment until cured.

clauses.title: Worker Classification Flow-Down
clauses.benchmark: Present in 31% of California services agreements; more common where the provider uses a contractor bench
clauses.rationale: A customer can inherit joint employer exposure for a provider's misclassified workforce, and the indemnity is the only practical protection.
clauses.body: The {{selfLabel}} represents that individuals performing the Services are properly classified under California law, including the [[ABC test|abc test]] where it applies, that all wages, overtime, meal and rest premiums, and business expense reimbursements have been paid, and that required workers' compensation coverage is in place. The {{selfLabel}} shall indemnify the {{counterLabel}} against claims arising from misclassification of its personnel, and this indemnity sits within the carve-outs at <<xr:msa_liability_carveouts>>.
